newsitem.title: CHINA: WEEK AHEAD - Hong Kong stocks seen pushed lower.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Hong Kong stocks seen pushed lower.

text.p: Currency jitters, property market concerns and overvaluations in the banking sector could push Hong Kong stocks lower this week, but China plays will continue to attract good interest, analysts and brokers said.
"This week will be an interesting, crucial time," said Frederick Tsang, head of research at BNP PrimeEast Securities.
Investors will be watching Hong Kong dollar currency rates and overnight lending rates for any signs of speculation and hedging, Tsang said.

The Hang Seng Index closed 51.11 points, or 0.33 percent, lower at 15,658.12 on Friday after hitting an all-time high of 15,880.57 on Thursday. Over the week the index gained 87.72 points or 0.56 percent.
Asia's central bankers met in Shanghai on Friday following several weeks of speculation against Asian currencies.
In a statement following the one-day meeting, the "Shanghai 11" said the region's economies were fundamentally sound and that they will work with the International Monetary Fund to aid members.
They also agreed to renew currency swap accords, which provide short-term liquidity to ease temporary balance of payment needs.
Hong Kong's monetary authority said on Friday that it was not worried about speculative attacks on the Hong Kong dollar.
The normally staid Hong Kong dollar has shown some volatility lately, while key lending rates in the territory have surged amid worries about the currency.
Stock market analysts said the finance sector could come under more selling pressure after an exuberant pre-results rally earlier in the month.
The Bank of East Asia will lead off the sector's reporting season on August 1. Analysts expect the bank to report earnings growth of about 16 percent for the first six months of 1997.
"The growth will be derived partly from lower provisions for bad and doubtful debts," said a banking analyst with a European brokerage.
The property sector is likely to remain subdued, analysts said.
"We think property developers are expecting a prolonged consolidation in residential property prices," said Tsang.
China-related issues will continue to be the focus of a broad segment of the market.
China Southern, the latest H-share to come to the market, will begin trading on Thursday and brokers said there was keen interest in the issue.
"We expect it to be priced in the top end of the range," said one U.S. trader. The indicative range is HK$3.71 to HK$4.70 per share.
